sentenceSets.sentence: His erudition was genuine rather than performed; he used it to illuminate problems rather than to impress.

answerChoices.reasoning: Intelligence is native quickness of mind, but the sentence describes a possession that could be performed for effect, which points to accumulated learning that can be displayed rather than to raw ability.
Expertise is command of one field, while nothing in the sentence limits what he knows to a specialty; the contrast is between deep reading used honestly and knowledge paraded.
Sophistication is worldly polish, and the sentence contrasts show with use in solving problems, which turns on substance of learning rather than on manner.
Eloquence is skill in speaking, and a merely eloquent man could not illuminate problems the way the sentence credits him with doing.
Confidence is self-assurance, which would be as compatible with performance as with genuineness and so misses the contrast the sentence draws.
Diligence is steady effort, and effort is not the sort of thing one performs in order to impress an audience mid-discussion.
A reputation exists in other people's minds and cannot be applied to illuminate a problem.
Curiosity is an appetite for knowing rather than the store of knowledge the sentence says he puts to work.
Ignorance could neither be genuine in the sense meant nor used to illuminate anything.
Arrogance is the failing the sentence says he avoids by not seeking to impress.
Idleness contradicts a man putting what he knows to work on problems.

sentenceSets.sentence: The footnotes alone display an erudition that the argument itself never quite exploits, citing four languages to make a point about one town.

answerChoices.reasoning: Thoroughness would mean nothing was left out, but the sentence marvels at the range of languages and reading on show rather than at completeness of coverage.
Pedantry is fussing over trivial correctness, whereas the footnotes are described as displaying real command of four languages that the argument fails to use.
Industry names the labor of assembling the notes, while the sentence is impressed by the depth of learning the notes reveal.
Fluency concerns ease in speaking or writing a language, and the point being made is about the breadth of scholarly reading behind a single local claim.
Obscurity is a fault of unclear writing, and the sentence's complaint is that the argument underuses what the notes contain, not that the prose is murky.
Arrogance would be an attitude toward readers, while the sentence's observation is about the learning stacked in the apparatus.
Precision concerns exactness of statement, which four languages cited for one town does not illustrate.
Brevity is contradicted by footnotes ranging across four languages for a single point.
Carelessness cannot be displayed by notes drawing on four languages.
Illiteracy is incompatible with citing sources in four languages.
Silence is not something footnotes can display through citation.

sentenceSets.sentence: The old bookseller's erudition was the sort acquired behind a counter, unsystematic but astonishing on any subject a customer happened to raise.

answerChoices.reasoning: Memory is the faculty of retention, but what astonishes customers is the store of learning itself, which the sentence traces to years spent among books.
Shrewdness is practical cunning, useful behind a counter for pricing stock, and it would not astonish a customer who raised an unexpected subject.
Patter is the fluent talk of a salesman, whereas the sentence stresses that the man could meet any subject a customer raised, which requires substance and not delivery.
Instinct is unlearned response, and the sentence explicitly describes something acquired over time behind the counter.
An inventory is the stock on his shelves rather than the knowledge in his head, and it could not be described as unsystematic yet astonishing on any subject.
Courtesy is a manner toward customers and would not vary with the subject raised.
Patience explains why he tolerates browsers, not why he can speak to any topic they bring up.
Solvency is a financial condition of the shop and has no connection to what he knows.
Ignorance is contradicted by a man who astonishes customers on whatever subject arises.
Indifference would keep him from engaging the subjects customers raise at all.
Forgetfulness is the opposite of the ready command the sentence describes.
